text: So what happened?
speaker: Narrator

text: And what does the biggest collection of stolen data ever discovered have to do with databases?
speaker: Narrator

text: In early 2024, security researchers discovered an enormous collection of stolen information that became known as the Mother of All Breaches, or MOAB.
speaker: Narrator

text: To find out, we'll have to go back to the beginning.
speaker: Narrator

text: Before we can understand how billions of records ended up in one place, we need to understand what a database actually is.
speaker: Narrator

text: It’s a good question, and the answer starts with your email account.
speaker: Narrator

text: If you had a Yahoo account, Yahoo had to keep track of information about you.
speaker: Narrator

text: Your name, your email address, your phone number, your date of birth, your password information, even your security questions.
speaker: Narrator

text: Each individual piece of information is called a field. Put those fields together, and you have a record.
speaker: Narrator

text: So every Yahoo account created another record that Yahoo had to store and manage.
speaker: Narrator

text: And when you’re dealing with hundreds of millions, or eventually billions, of accounts, you need a system built to organize all of that information. That system is a database.
speaker: Narrator

text: And having all that information stored is only useful if you can actually find what you need.
speaker: Narrator

text: Say you type your Yahoo email address into the login screen. Yahoo doesn’t scroll through millions of accounts looking for yours. It asks the database for the record that matches.
speaker: Narrator

text: That request is called a query.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “And Yahoo had another problem. A lot of people were doing this at the same time.
speaker: Narrator

text: Databases are built for concurrent use, meaning lots of people can access the same system at once. That’s one reason a company like Yahoo needs a database instead of one enormous spreadsheet.”     Database vs spreadsheet
speaker: Narrator

text: “Then there’s size.
speaker: Narrator

text: As more people sign up, the database has to grow with them. That ability to keep handling more and more information is called scalability.
speaker: Narrator

text: Thousands of records can become millions. Millions can become billions.”     databases
speaker: Narrator

text: “But there’s one question we haven’t asked yet.
speaker: Narrator

text: Who is allowed to see all of it?”
speaker: Narrator

text: “Databases use permissions to control access. One person might be allowed to see information. Another might be allowed to change it. Someone else might not be allowed in at all.”     databases
speaker: Narrator

text: “And that brings us back to Yahoo.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “In 2013, someone who wasn’t supposed to have access got access to Yahoo account data.
speaker: Narrator

text: Eventually, Yahoo revealed that every account it had at the time had been affected.
speaker: Narrator

text: About three billion accounts.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “Three billion sounded enormous.
speaker: Narrator

text: But Yahoo was only one breach.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “Over the years, stolen records from Yahoo and thousands of other breaches kept circulating.
speaker: Narrator

text: Some were usernames. Some were email addresses. Some contained passwords or other account information.
speaker: Narrator

text: And eventually, huge collections of that stolen data started getting combined.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “Which brings us to 2024.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “Researchers uncovered a collection so large it was nicknamed the Mother of All Breaches — MOAB.
speaker: Narrator

text: About 26 billion records.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “But here’s the important part.
speaker: Narrator

text: That does not mean 26 billion people were hacked in one giant attack.
speaker: Narrator

text: MOAB was largely a collection of records from earlier breaches gathered together in one place.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “And now that we know what a record is, that number makes a little more sense.
speaker: Narrator

text: The same person can have a Yahoo account, a social media account, a shopping account, and dozens of other accounts.
speaker: Narrator

text: One person can appear in many different records.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “But putting billions of records together creates something powerful.
speaker: Narrator

text: Remember queries?
speaker: Narrator

text: Once information is organized, it can be searched.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “That’s what makes databases so useful to businesses. They don’t just hold information. They make enormous amounts of information easier to find, update, organize, and use.”     databases
speaker: Narrator

text: “And the same thing that makes a database useful can make stolen data dangerous.
speaker: Narrator

text: A pile of random information is one thing.
speaker: Narrator

text: Billions of organized, searchable records are something else.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “That doesn’t make databases bad technology. Almost every organization depends on them.
speaker: Narrator

text: Stores use them for customers and inventory. Banks use them for accounts and transactions. Streaming services use them to keep track of users and content. Even your email account depends on one.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “The lesson from Yahoo and MOAB is really about scale.
speaker: Narrator

text: One field becomes part of a record.
speaker: Narrator

text: Records fill a database.
speaker: Narrator

text: Databases can grow to serve millions or billions of users.
speaker: Narrator

text: And when that much information is collected in one place, managing who can access it becomes just as important as storing it.”
speaker: Narrator

text: “So the next time you log into your email, there’s a lot more happening behind that little password box than it looks like.”
speaker: Narrator
